standard_prerequisites.name: An object of projective amplitude in an interval is represented by a complex of projective modules vanishing outside that interval, and a perfect object of tor amplitude there is represented by finite projective modules
standard_prerequisites.use: Provides the representative of the first object in the vanishing computation, in both the general and the perfect case.

standard_prerequisites.name: An object whose cohomology vanishes above a bound is quasi-isomorphic to its truncation below that bound, hence representable by a complex vanishing there
standard_prerequisites.use: Puts the second object in the form in which no nonzero map of complexes into it can exist.

standard_prerequisites.name: Maps in the derived category from a bounded complex of projectives are maps of complexes, and a distinguished triangle whose first Hom group vanishes splits
standard_prerequisites.use: Gives assertion (1), then the splitting of the triangle in assertion (2) and the uniqueness in assertion (3).

core_obligations: Use the hypothesis on projective amplitude to represent the first object by a complex of projective modules vanishing outside the given interval, invoking the definition of projective dimension, or by a complex of finite projective modules in the perfect case (proof lines 19720-19727).

Assume the cohomology of the second object vanishes above the lower end of the interval, replace it by its truncation and hence by a complex vanishing there, and compute that there are no nonzero maps of complexes from the first representative to the second, which proves assertion (1) (proof lines 19727-19734).

For assertion (2), apply assertion (1) to the shift of the second object to see that the relevant Hom group vanishes, and conclude from the splitting criterion for distinguished triangles that the middle object is isomorphic to the direct sum of the two outer ones compatibly with the maps of the triangle (proof lines 19734-19738).

For assertion (3), use the vanishing of assertion (1) again to see that a morphism between the two objects must be zero, which makes the splitting isomorphism of assertion (2) unique (proof lines 19738-19740).
proof_roadmap: Represent both objects by complexes of the appropriate shape using projective amplitude and the vanishing of cohomology (proof lines 19720-19731).
Get the vanishing of the Hom group from the disjointness of the supports of the representatives (proof lines 19731-19734).
Split the distinguished triangle and deduce uniqueness from the same vanishing (proof lines 19734-19740).
difficulty_reason: The statement draws three consequences from a projective amplitude hypothesis on one object of the derived category: maps from it into a complex whose cohomology vanishes high enough are zero, every distinguished triangle with it as the third term splits, and in the strongest case the splitting is unique (statement lines 19703-19718). The proof chooses representatives adapted to both hypotheses, so that the two complexes have disjoint supports, reads off the vanishing of the Hom group through the identification of maps from a bounded complex of projectives, and then applies the splitting criterion of triangulated categories, with uniqueness coming from the same vanishing applied to a morphism of the split triangle (proof lines 19720-19740). The choice of representatives is what reduces all three assertions to one computation.
